# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

There is a common picture of what a successful meeting looks like: a room full of people who began with different views and ended, through discussion and compromise, in harmony. Someone sums up the mood, everyone nods, and the meeting adjourns with a satisfying sense of closure. Agreement, in this picture, is the goal. Disagreement is the obstacle to be overcome on the way there.

But this picture deserves scrutiny. Agreement is not always a sign that a problem has been solved. Sometimes it is a sign that a problem has been papered over—that people have stopped arguing not because they've converged on the truth, but because they've grown tired, or because the most senior person in the room has signaled a preference, or because nobody wants to be the one who prolongs a meeting that was supposed to end at noon. Genuine agreement is valuable. Performed agreement is dangerous, because it hides the very thing that needs attention.
